extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century periodical readers; theatre-goers, writers, and those interested in manners and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essays offering literary and social criticism aimed at improving public taste — specifically commentary on theatre, poetry, and modes of conversation. The pieces mix news, satire, prescriptive remarks, and examples to show what counts as good or bad practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of behaviour as perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of behaviour, which is the perfection of good breeding and good sense, is utterly lost in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, natural behaviour and conversation as the mark of good breeding and sense; avoid affectations and contrived refinements that replace genuine wit. The text contrasts simplicity with numerous artificial inventions that pass for wit among the fashionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'biter' conversational vice
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Biter' is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself ... and if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not practice or celebrate biting (deceptive, contemptuous witticisms). The essay contrasts the biter (a contemptible impostor) with the droll (a pleasant, natural wit) and treats the biter as an anti-pattern of modern conversation; dramatists can expose this folly on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should be governed by judges of talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and spirit, humour and good sense, can never be revived, but under the government of those who are judges of such talents, who know, that whatever is put up in their stead, is but a short and trifling expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The selection and management of theatre must be entrusted to knowledgeable judges who can recognise genuine talent and taste, rather than managers motivated solely by profit or novelty. Without such stewardship, temporary expedients (spectacle, songs, dances) will supplant substantive drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize action and genuine wit over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: When the seat of wit was thus mortgaged ... instead of action there, we have been put off by song and dance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works should emphasize enacted plot and character (action, wit, humour) rather than relying on ladder-dancers, rope-dancers, jugglers, or other spectacles. Such substitutes are a degradation of the stage and a short-lived expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject inauthentic imported performers and false vocal tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: This latter help of sound has also begun to fail for want of voices; therefore the palace has since been put into the hands of a surgeon, who cuts any foreign fellow into an eunuch, and passes him upon us for a singer of Italy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of importing or manufacturing performers (e.g., castrati) presented as authentic singers when they lack true vocal quality. Authentic vocal ability and appropriate casting are necessary; surgical or artificial gimmicks to supply 'singers of Italy' are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as moral and social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: It is now some years since several revolutions in the gay world had made the empire of the stage subject to very fatal convulsions ... The theatre has much the same effect on the manners of the age, as the bank on the credit of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the stage as having real social influence — plays should aim to correct or reflect manners and morals. Managers and playwrights have responsibility because theatre shapes public taste and behaviour; neglecting that responsibility harms public morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should employ vivid, descriptive imagery that prompts reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Such images as these give us a new pleasure in our sight, and fix upon our minds traces of reflection, which accompany us whenever the like objects occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good descriptive poetry (example: Philips' winter poem) uses striking, exact images that stay with the reader and stimulate thought. Excellent description not only pleases but trains readers to think and appreciate 'men of wit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction must be natural and properly rhymed
rubrics_metrics.description: Avail and toil, defect and tract, will never do for rhymes. ... he has the true spirit in him; for which reason I was willing to entertain anything he pleased to send me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forced, awkward rhymes and strained diction. Poetic imagery must be controlled and directed; enthusiasm or warmth without disciplined expression leads to bad rhyme and phrasing. The author critiques specific awkward rhyme-choices as instructive anti-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use satire and allegory on stage to expose social/political truths
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first he has represented absolute power, in the person of a tall man with a hat and feather, who gives his first minister ... a huge kick ... This latter performance he makes to be the representation of a free state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ allegory, dance, and moralised humour to make political and social points effectively: e.g., a staged dance representing the transmission of kicks illustrates absolute vs. free government. Well-crafted stage allegory can instruct and amuse simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should depict contemporary social types for moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: As these new creatures appear in the world, it might give an excellent field to writers for the stage, to divert us with the representation of them there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and poets should turn current social follies and characters (rakes, gamesters, biters, mountebanks) into dramatic material to satirize and reform manners; the stage is an appropriate venue for social diagnosis and correction.
